newsitem.title: GERMANY: Lufthansa seeks record results in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Lufthansa seeks record results in 1997.

text.p: Lufthansa AG said on Thursday it would end the first half of 1997 with profits significantly higher than in the 1995 and 1996 periods amid strong passenger growth at the German airline.
Lufthansa also said its 1997 results could top its record 1995 results -- provided industry conditions do not change.
"Lufthansa is off to a pleasing start in 1997," Lufthansa Chairman Juergen Weber said in a statement at the airline's annual general meeting.

"In the absence of major changes in the market, we expect 1997 results to be above the best-ever results in 1995," Weber said. He also noted that oil prices were not expected to rise during the rest of the year.
Weber said Lufthansa's first-half results, to be released on August 26, would top results during the same periods in 1995 and 1996 and exceeded the airline's own expectations.
"We will end the first half of this year with profits significantly higher than the prior-year level and also above the good half-year results in 1995," he said.
"The barometer is presently rising. Our passenger numbers are growing strongly, especially in the North Atlantic, Asian and Pacific markets," Weber said.

Passenger traffic on South American routes has recently been up about nine percent, while North American traffic has been up 8.5 percent. But Weber said the German market has failed to show much improvement.
"Demand so far this year has been lively," he said of flights to North and South America. "It has never been so good."
Weber also said results in Lufthansa's cargo business "are improving distinctly".

Lufthansa in 1996 reported a profit from ordinary activities of 686 million marks on sales of 20.8 billion marks. In 1995, Lufthansa had a profit from ordinary activities of 756 million marks on sales of 19.9 billion marks.

Lufthansa had hoped to have record earnings in 1996 but those hopes were foiled by higher fuel and operating costs, which Weber said rose eight percent to 22.2 billion marks and rose faster than said.
He also noted that the airline's fuel costs in 1996 rose 22 pecent to 1.8 billion marks due to surging world oil prices in the second half of the year.
Weber also said Lufthansa would keep up its cost-cutting measures, which he said aim to cut 1.5 billion marks, or 20 percent, in the airline's operating costs.
The airline has already identified 50 projects that could save up to 900 million marks by 1999, Weber said.
